analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare's payments for prescription drugs at the lowest price the federal government already pays through the VA or GSA.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2023 and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what Medicare pays for every drug covered under Part B and Part D at the lower of the prices the Department of Veterans Affairs or the federal supply schedule pays for that drug. Since seniors' copays and coinsurance are calculated from the price Medicare pays, capping Medicare's payment would directly cut what beneficiaries pay out of pocket. Drugmakers would have to accept those prices as a condition of having their drugs covered by Medicare at all. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's roughly 65 million beneficiaries, especially seniors who take expensive brand-name drugs, would pay less out of pocket because their copays and coinsurance are calculated as a share of what Medicare pays. Taxpayers would also benefit from a smaller federal Medicare bill.

how_it_helps.text: For every drug covered by Medicare Part B (drugs given in a doctor's office) and Part D (prescriptions filled at a pharmacy), Medicare could not pay more than the lower of what the VA or the GSA Federal Supply Schedule pays for that drug.
Drug manufacturers would have to agree to charge no more than that capped amount as a condition of having their drugs covered by Medicare at all.
Because seniors' cost-sharing (their copays and coinsurance) is calculated as a share of what Medicare pays, capping Medicare's payment lowers what beneficiaries themselves pay out of pocket.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would see sharply lower Medicare revenue, and through them, pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers who take a cut of drug prices would see their margins squeezed.

drawbacks.text: By forcing manufacturers to sell to Medicare at VA/GSA prices as a condition of coverage, the bill would cut into the revenue drug companies earn from the U.S. market, which the industry says funds research and development into new medicines.

Tying Medicare payment to prices set in separate procurement systems (VA and GSA) is a blunt mechanism; if those prices are not representative of the broader market, it could create payment disruptions for pharmacies and plans, and would likely draw legal challenges over whether the government can condition participation on such price agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—lower out-of-pocket drug costs for seniors and savings to Medicare—is large and direct. The drawback is real: tying Medicare prices to what other federal agencies pay, which have far less purchasing power than the full Medicare program, could disrupt pharmacy payment systems and face court challenges from manufacturers; many economists argue bulk-purchasing-style caps can reduce revenues available for research. But the bill was never even considered, so no tradeoff was ever weighed on its merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, vote, or floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on May 4, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, whose jurisdiction covers Medicare.
No further action was taken: the record shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no Senate floor consideration before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, so it never had the support needed to force action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who keep charging Medicare and its beneficiaries prices far above the government's own procurement rates. Seniors continue to pay the difference at the pharmacy counter.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (VT), Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap Medicare drug prices at the lower of VA or GSA procurement prices.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Joined as a cosponsor of the bill.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Long opposed price caps tied to government procurement prices; the industry generally lobbies against such measures and works to keep them from advancing.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress—no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a progressive sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no record of broader party positioning exists; there is no recorded Republican support.

industries.note: The bill would require drugmakers to sell to Medicare at the government's best negotiated procurement price, cutting revenue on Part B and Part D drugs. Manufacturers would have to accept those prices to keep Medicare coverage at all.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers
industries.note: Caps on the negotiated price of Part D drugs would shrink the spread these intermediaries and insurers manage on Medicare drug plans.
Lower drug payment benchmarks reduce reimbursement tied to drug costs, but pharmacies and prescribers would also benefit from patients affording and filling more prescriptions.
